paper.title: Expected TGT paper 3 · harder, 2021 level
paper.source: Written by GS HOUSE for the UP TGT Mathematics exam expected in December 2026, in the pattern of the UP TGT paper of 3 June 2026 and the official syllabus: 30 questions asked in earlier papers (15 from UP TGT 2010 and 15 from UP TGT 2013; each solved again, misprints repaired) and 60 new; every question checked by a second mathematician

en.q: The roots of $x^3 - 9x^2 + 23x - 15 = 0$ are in A.P. The roots are:
en.explanation: Let the roots be $a - d, a, a + d$. Sum: $3a = 9 \Rightarrow a = 3$. Product: $a(a^2 - d^2) = 15 \Rightarrow 9 - d^2 = 5 \Rightarrow d = \pm 2$. Roots $1, 3, 5$ (check: $1\cdot3 + 3\cdot5 + 5\cdot1 = 23$).
notes: Sum is right but the product is −21.
Sum is right (9) but the product is 24, not 15.
Takes the middle root as 15/3 = 5 (from the constant term); then the sum is 15, not 9.
path: 1.8 Quadratic equations and theory of equations
facts: For roots in A.P. take $a-d, a, a+d$: the sum of the roots fixes $a$ at once.

en.q: The acute angle between the curves $y^2 = 4x$ and $x^2 = 4y$ at their point of intersection other than the origin is:
en.explanation: Intersection: $x^2 = 4y$ gives $y = \frac{x^2}{4}$, so $\frac{x^4}{16} = 4x \Rightarrow x = 0$ or $x = 4$; the other point is $(4, 4)$. $y^2 = 4x \Rightarrow y' = \frac2y = \frac12$ at $(4,4)$. $x^2 = 4y \Rightarrow y' = \frac x2 = 2$. $\tan\theta = \left|\frac{2 - \frac12}{1 + 2\cdot\frac12}\right| = \frac{3/2}{2} = \frac34$, so $\theta = \tan^{-1}\frac34$.
notes: This is the angle at the origin, where the tangents are the two axes.
Inverts the formula (this is the cotangent).
Adds the slopes instead of subtracting.
facts: Angle between curves = angle between their tangents at the common point.

en.q: If $A$ is a skew-symmetric matrix, then $A^2$ is:
en.explanation: $A^T = -A$, so $(A^2)^T = (A^T)^2 = (-A)^2 = A^2$. Hence $A^2$ is symmetric. (For $A = \begin{bmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{bmatrix}$, $A^2 = -I$, which is symmetric but neither zero nor $I$.)
facts: $(A^n)^T = (A^T)^n$; even powers of a skew-symmetric matrix are symmetric, odd powers skew-symmetric.

en.q: The modal class of a frequency distribution is 40–50 with frequency 16; the classes just before and just after it have frequencies 10 and 12. The mode is:
notes: The class mark of the modal class, not the mode given by the formula.
Forgets to multiply by the class width: $40 + 0.6$.
Uses $f_1 - f_2 = 4$ in the numerator instead of $f_1 - f_0 = 6$.
facts: Mode of grouped data $= l + \frac{f_1 - f_0}{2f_1 - f_0 - f_2} \times h$, where $f_0$ and $f_2$ are the frequencies of the classes just before and after the modal class.

en.q: The centre of gravity of a uniform solid right circular cone of height $h$ lies on its axis at a height above the base of:
en.explanation: Slices parallel to the base at height $y$ have mass proportional to $(h - y)^2$. $\bar y = \frac{\int_0^h y(h-y)^2\,dy}{\int_0^h (h-y)^2\,dy} = \frac{h^4/12}{h^3/3} = \frac h4$ (i.e. $\frac{3h}{4}$ from the vertex).
notes: This is for a hollow cone (or a triangular lamina).
This is for a solid hemisphere (from its centre).
facts: C.G. above the base: solid cone $h/4$, hollow cone $h/3$; solid hemisphere $3r/8$ from the centre.

src.label: Expected TGT 3 · Q6 · asked in UP TGT 2013

en.q: P and R can do a work in 30 days, P and Q can do the same work in 45 days while Q and R can do the same work in 60 days. Then in how many days can only R do this work?
en.explanation: Let the one-day works be $p, q, r$: $p+r=\frac1{30}$, $p+q=\frac1{45}$, $q+r=\frac1{60}$. Adding, $2(p+q+r)=\frac{6+4+3}{180}=\frac{13}{180}$, so $p+q+r=\frac{13}{360}$. Then $r=\frac{13}{360}-\frac{1}{45}=\frac{13-8}{360}=\frac{1}{72}$: R alone takes 72 days.
notes: This is the time of P and Q together, read off the data.
facts: With three pair-rates, add them: the sum is twice the rate of all three working together.

src.label: Expected TGT 3 · Q7 · asked in UP TGT 2010

en.q: The values of $x, y, z$ by Cramer's rule from the equations $x + y + z = 4$, $2x - y + 2z = 5$ and $x - 2y - z = -3$ are:
notes: Right numbers in the wrong order: fails the third equation.
path: 2.4 Rank and systems of linear equations
facts: Cramer: $x = D_x/D$, $y = D_y/D$, $z = D_z/D$ when $D \ne 0$.

en.q: In a triangle $ABC$, $a = \sqrt3 + 1$, $b = \sqrt3 - 1$ and $C = 60^\circ$. Then $A - B$ equals:
en.explanation: Napier's analogy: $\tan\frac{A-B}{2} = \frac{a-b}{a+b}\cot\frac C2 = \frac{2}{2\sqrt3}\cot30^\circ = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}\cdot\sqrt3 = 1$. So $\frac{A-B}{2} = 45^\circ$, $A - B = 90^\circ$ (with $A + B = 120^\circ$: $A = 105^\circ$, $B = 15^\circ$).
facts: Napier's analogy: $\tan\frac{A-B}{2} = \frac{a-b}{a+b}\cot\frac{C}{2}$.

src.label: Expected TGT 3 · Q9 · asked in UP TGT 2010

en.q: Vectors $2\hat i - \hat j + \hat k$, $\hat i + 2\hat j - 3\hat k$ and $3\hat i + p\hat j + 5\hat k$ are coplanar. Then $p$ is:
en.explanation: Coplanar $\iff$ scalar triple product $= 0$: $\begin{vmatrix}2&-1&1\\1&2&-3\\3&p&5\end{vmatrix} = 2(10 + 3p) + 1(5 + 9) + 1(p - 6) = 7p + 28 = 0 \Rightarrow p = -4$.
facts: Three vectors are coplanar iff $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c] = 0$.

src.label: Expected TGT 3 · Q10 · asked in UP TGT 2010

en.q: The equation of the sphere which passes through the origin and the points of intersection of the plane $\frac xa + \frac yb + \frac zc = 1$ with the coordinate axes is:
en.explanation: The plane meets the axes at $(a,0,0)$, $(0,b,0)$, $(0,0,c)$. Take $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + 2ux + 2vy + 2wz + d = 0$. Through $O$: $d = 0$. Through $(a,0,0)$: $a^2 + 2ua = 0 \Rightarrow 2u = -a$; similarly $2v = -b$, $2w = -c$. Sphere: $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - ax - by - cz = 0$.
facts: Sphere through $O$ and the intercepts $(a,0,0), (0,b,0), (0,0,c)$: $x^2+y^2+z^2 = ax+by+cz$.

en.q: If $\alpha, \beta$ are the roots of $x^2 - px + q = 0$, then $\frac{\alpha}{\beta} + \frac{\beta}{\alpha}$ equals:
en.explanation: $\alpha + \beta = p$, $\alpha\beta = q$. $\frac\alpha\beta + \frac\beta\alpha = \frac{\alpha^2+\beta^2}{\alpha\beta} = \frac{(\alpha+\beta)^2 - 2\alpha\beta}{\alpha\beta} = \frac{p^2 - 2q}{q}$.
path: 1.8 Quadratic equations and theory of equations
facts: $\alpha^2 + \beta^2 = (\alpha+\beta)^2 - 2\alpha\beta$.

options: Reflexive and transitive but not symmetric
Reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
Reflexive but neither symmetric nor transitive
en.explanation: All of $(1,1), (2,2), (3,3)$ are in $R$: reflexive. $(1,2) \in R$ but $(2,1) \notin R$: not symmetric. $(1,2), (2,3) \in R$ but $(1,3) \notin R$: not transitive.
facts: To disprove transitivity find $(a,b), (b,c) \in R$ with $(a,c) \notin R$.

en.q: $\int\frac{dx}{(x^2 + 1)(x^2 + 4)}$ is equal to:
en.explanation: Partial fractions in $x^2$: $\frac{1}{(x^2+1)(x^2+4)} = \frac13\left[\frac{1}{x^2+1} - \frac{1}{x^2+4}\right]$. Integrating: $\frac13\tan^{-1}x - \frac13\cdot\frac12\tan^{-1}\frac x2 + c = \frac13\tan^{-1}x - \frac16\tan^{-1}\frac x2 + c$.
notes: Sign slip in the partial fractions.

en.q: The number of real solutions of the equation $\tan^{-1}\sqrt{x(x+1)}$ $+\sin^{-1}\sqrt{x^2+x+1}=\frac{\pi}{2}$ is:
en.explanation:
$\sqrt{x(x+1)}$ is real only if $x(x+1)\ge0$, and $\sin^{-1}\sqrt{x^2+x+1}$ needs $x^2+x+1\le1$, i.e. $x(x+1)\le0$.
So $x(x+1)=0$: $x=0$ or $x=-1$. For both, the left side is $\tan^{-1}0+\sin^{-1}1=\frac\pi2$.
Hence there are exactly 2 real solutions.
notes: Assumes $x^2+x+1>1$ always; it equals 1 at $x=0$ and $x=-1$.
Correct: the domain is $\{-1,0\}$ and both points satisfy the equation.
Treats it as an identity like $\tan^{-1}a+\cot^{-1}a=\frac\pi2$; both terms are defined together only at two points.
facts: Before solving an equation in inverse functions, find its domain: $\sin^{-1}u$ and $\cos^{-1}u$ need $|u|\le1$, and $\sqrt u$ needs $u\ge0$.

src.label: Expected TGT 3 · Q15 · asked in UP TGT 2010

en.q: The line $x\cos\alpha + y\sin\alpha = p$ will touch the parabola $y^2 = 4a(x + a)$, if:
en.explanation: Put $X = x + a$: the parabola is $y^2 = 4aX$ and the line is $X\cos\alpha + y\sin\alpha = p + a\cos\alpha$, i.e. $y = mX + c$ with $m = -\cot\alpha$, $c = \frac{p + a\cos\alpha}{\sin\alpha}$. Tangency: $c = \frac am = -\frac{a\sin\alpha}{\cos\alpha}$. So $(p + a\cos\alpha)\cos\alpha = -a\sin^2\alpha$, i.e. $p\cos\alpha + a = 0$.
facts: $y = mx + c$ touches $y^2 = 4ax$ iff $c = a/m$.

src.label: Expected TGT 3 · Q16 · asked in UP TGT 2013

en.q: The value of $\left(\frac{\cos\theta + i\sin\theta}{i\cos\theta + \sin\theta}\right)^4$ will be:
en.explanation: $\sin\theta + i\cos\theta = i(\cos\theta - i\sin\theta) = ie^{-i\theta}$. The ratio is $\frac{e^{i\theta}}{ie^{-i\theta}} = -ie^{2i\theta}$, and its 4th power is $(-i)^4e^{8i\theta} = \cos8\theta + i\sin8\theta$.
notes: Ignores the denominator: this is only $(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^4$.
path: 10.4 Polar form, Euler's form and De Moivre's theorem
facts: $\sin\theta + i\cos\theta = i e^{-i\theta}$; $(-i)^4 = 1$.

src.label: Expected TGT 3 · Q17 · asked in UP TGT 2010

en.q: If $\log_\ell x$, $\log_m x$ and $\log_n x$ are in A.P., then the value of $n^2$ is (where $x \ne 1$):
en.explanation: $\log_k x = \frac{\log x}{\log k}$. A.P.: $\frac{2}{\log m} = \frac{1}{\log\ell} + \frac{1}{\log n}$, so $2\log\ell\log n = \log m(\log\ell + \log n) = \log m \cdot \log(\ell n)$. Dividing by $\log\ell$: $2\log n = \log_\ell m \cdot \log(\ell n)$, i.e. $\log n^2 = \log(\ell n)^{\log_\ell m}$. Hence $n^2 = (\ell n)^{\log_\ell m}$.
notes: Wrong pair of bases with a natural logarithm: for $\ell = 2$, $n = 8$ (then $m = 2\sqrt2$) it is about 8.7, not $n^2 = 64$.
For $\ell = 2$, $n = 8$, $m = 2\sqrt2$: $\log_m n = 2$, so this is $(16\sqrt2)^2 = 512$, not 64.
path: 1.6 Sequences and series: AP, GP, HP
facts: $\log_a x, \log_b x, \log_c x$ in A.P. $\iff$ $\frac1{\log a}, \frac1{\log b}, \frac1{\log c}$ in A.P.

en.q: The Cantor set, obtained from $[0, 1]$ by removing open middle thirds again and again, is:
en.explanation: Length removed $= \frac13 + \frac29 + \frac{4}{27} + \cdots = \frac{1/3}{1 - 2/3} = 1$, so the set left has total length $1 - 1 = 0$. Its points are the numbers of $[0, 1]$ with a ternary expansion using only the digits 0 and 2. Replacing each 2 by 1 and reading the digits in binary maps the set onto the whole of $[0, 1]$, so it is at least as large as $[0, 1]$: uncountable. (It is more than the endpoints: $\frac14 = 0.0202\ldots$ in base 3 is in it.)
notes: The endpoints of the removed intervals are countable, but the set has many other points, e.g. $\frac14$.
1 is the total length removed, not the length left.
Correct: length $1 - 1 = 0$, yet the set maps onto $[0, 1]$.
Both parts wrong: it is uncountable, and the length left is 0.
facts: The Cantor set is closed, perfect and uncountable, yet has total length (measure) 0.

src.label: Expected TGT 3 · Q19 · asked in UP TGT 2010

en.q: For what value of $x$, the mode of the following data is 7? 3, 5, 6, 7, 5, 4, 7, 5, 6, $x$, 8, 7
en.explanation: Without $x$, 5 occurs three times and 7 occurs three times (a tie). For 7 alone to be the mode, $x$ must be 7, so that 7 occurs four times.
notes: Then 5, 6 and 7 each occur three times: no single mode 7.
A value not in the data leaves 5 and 7 tied.
facts: The mode is the most frequent value; a tie gives more than one mode.

en.q: A chord of a circle of radius 13 cm is at a distance of 5 cm from the centre. The length of the chord is:
en.explanation: The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord. Half-chord $= \sqrt{13^2 - 5^2} = 12$ cm, so the chord is 24 cm.
facts: Chord length $= 2\sqrt{r^2 - d^2}$, $d$ = distance from the centre.

en.q: If $A$ is a square matrix such that $A^2 - A + I = O$, then $A^{-1}$ equals:
en.explanation: $A^2 - A + I = O \Rightarrow A^2 - A = -I \Rightarrow A(A - I) = -I \Rightarrow A(I - A) = I$. Hence $A$ is invertible and $A^{-1} = I - A$.
facts: From a polynomial relation in $A$ with non-zero constant term, factor out $A$ to read off $A^{-1}$.

en.q: The interior of the set $\mathbb{Q}$ of rational numbers, as a subset of $\mathbb{R}$, is:
en.explanation: A point $x$ is an interior point of $\mathbb{Q}$ if some interval $(x - \varepsilon, x + \varepsilon)$ lies inside $\mathbb{Q}$. Every interval contains irrational numbers (the irrationals are dense in $\mathbb{R}$), so no interval lies inside $\mathbb{Q}$ and no point is interior. Hence the interior of $\mathbb{Q}$ is $\varnothing$.
notes: $\mathbb{Q}$ is not open: no interval around a rational lies inside $\mathbb{Q}$.
$\mathbb{R}$ is the closure of $\mathbb{Q}$ ($\mathbb{Q}$ is dense), not its interior.
The interior of a set is part of the set; irrationals are not in $\mathbb{Q}$.
path: 5.3 Order properties, bounds and point-set topology of R
facts: In $\mathbb{R}$: the interior of $\mathbb{Q}$ is $\varnothing$, while its closure and its boundary are both $\mathbb{R}$.

en.q: The equation of the circle concentric with $x^2 + y^2 - 4x + 6y - 3 = 0$ and passing through the point $(1, 1)$ is:
en.explanation: A concentric circle has the same $x^2$, $y^2$, $x$ and $y$ terms and another constant: $x^2 + y^2 - 4x + 6y + c = 0$. It passes through $(1, 1)$: $1 + 1 - 4 + 6 + c = 0$, so $c = -4$. (Check: centre $(2, -3)$, $r^2 = 1^2 + 4^2 = 17$, and $c = 4 + 9 - 17 = -4$.)
notes: The signs of the $x$ and $y$ terms are reversed: that circle has centre $(-2, 3)$, not $(2, -3)$.
Sign slip in $c$: at $(1, 1)$ it gives $1 + 1 - 4 + 6 + 4 = 8 \ne 0$.
Puts $c = -r^2 = -17$, forgetting that $c = g^2 + f^2 - r^2 = 13 - 17$.
Correct: the same centre $(2, -3)$, with $c$ fixed by the point $(1, 1)$.
facts: Circles concentric with $x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0$ are $x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + k = 0$; one point of the circle fixes $k$.

src.label: Expected TGT 3 · Q24 · asked in UP TGT 2013

en.q: If $|\vec a| = 5$, $|\vec a - \vec b| = 8$ and $|\vec a + \vec b| = 10$, then what will be the value of $|\vec b|$?
en.explanation: Parallelogram law: $|\vec a + \vec b|^2 + |\vec a - \vec b|^2 = 2(|\vec a|^2 + |\vec b|^2)$. $100 + 64 = 2(25 + |\vec b|^2) \Rightarrow |\vec b|^2 = 57 \Rightarrow |\vec b| = \sqrt{57}$.
facts: $|\vec a+\vec b|^2 + |\vec a-\vec b|^2 = 2(|\vec a|^2 + |\vec b|^2)$.

src.label: Expected TGT 3 · Q25 · asked in UP TGT 2010

en.q: The equation of the normal at $(3, -2)$ on the ellipse $4x^2 + 9y^2 = 72$ is:
en.explanation: Differentiating, $8x + 18yy' = 0 \Rightarrow y' = -\frac{4x}{9y} = -\frac{12}{-18} = \frac23$ at $(3,-2)$. Normal slope $= -\frac32$: $y + 2 = -\frac32(x - 3) \Rightarrow 3x + 2y = 5$.
notes: Slope $+\frac32$ instead of $-\frac32$; it does not even pass through $(3, -2)$, since $9 + 4 \ne 5$.
This is the tangent at $(3, -2)$, not the normal.
Sign of the constant wrong: $(3, -2)$ does not lie on it.
facts: Normal slope $= -1/(\text{tangent slope})$; the normal passes through the given point.

en.q: The positive square root of $11 - 6\sqrt2$ is:
en.explanation: Write $11 - 6\sqrt2 = 9 + 2 - 2 \cdot 3 \cdot \sqrt2 = (3 - \sqrt2)^2$. Since $3 > \sqrt2$, the positive square root is $3 - \sqrt2$.
facts: $\sqrt{a + b - 2\sqrt{ab}} = \sqrt a - \sqrt b$ for $a > b > 0$: find two numbers with sum $a + b$ and product $ab$.

en.q: The compound interest on ₹10,000 for 2 years at 10% per annum, compounded half-yearly, is:
notes: This uses 2.5% for 8 periods (quarterly), the wrong period.
This is the interest compounded annually.
facts: Compounded half-yearly: halve the rate and double the number of periods.

en.q: For the conic $\frac{10}{r} = 5 + 4\cos\theta$, the eccentricity $e$ and the semi-latus rectum $l$ are:
en.explanation: The standard form is $\frac lr = 1 + e\cos\theta$. Dividing by 5: $\frac2r = 1 + \frac45\cos\theta$. Hence $e = \frac45$ (an ellipse) and $l = 2$.
notes: Reads the coefficients without making the constant term 1.
Divides only the right side by 5.
path: 11.8 Polar equation of a conic; common tangents (PGT)
facts: Make the constant term 1 before reading $e$ and $l$ from $\frac lr = 1 + e\cos\theta$.

src.label: Expected TGT 3 · Q29 · asked in UP TGT 2013

en.q: If $xy = a^2$ and $s = b^2x + c^2y$, where $a$, $b$, $c$ are positive constants and $x, y > 0$, then the minimum value of $s$ will be:
en.explanation: $s = b^2x + \frac{a^2c^2}{x}$ ($x > 0$). $\frac{ds}{dx} = b^2 - \frac{a^2c^2}{x^2} = 0 \Rightarrow x = \frac{ac}{b}$, and $\frac{d^2s}{dx^2} = \frac{2a^2c^2}{x^3} > 0$: minimum. $s_{\min} = b^2\cdot\frac{ac}{b} + \frac{a^2c^2b}{ac} = 2abc$. (Or AM ≥ GM: $b^2x + c^2y \ge 2\sqrt{b^2c^2xy} = 2abc$.) (The original says only "constants"; without $x, y > 0$, $s$ has no least value, so the condition is stated.)
notes: Value of each of the two equal terms, not their sum.
facts: For $xy$ fixed, $px + qy$ is least when $px = qy$ (AM ≥ GM).

en.q: A particle is projected so that its horizontal range is $4\sqrt3$ times its greatest height. The angle of projection is:
en.explanation: $R = \frac{2u^2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha}{g}$ and $H = \frac{u^2\sin^2\alpha}{2g}$, so $\frac RH = 4\cot\alpha$. $4\cot\alpha = 4\sqrt3 \Rightarrow \cot\alpha = \sqrt3 \Rightarrow \alpha = 30^\circ$.
facts: $R = 4H\cot\alpha$ for a projectile on a horizontal plane.

en.q: $\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\sqrt{n^2 + n} - n\right)$ equals:
en.explanation: Multiply and divide by $\sqrt{n^2+n} + n$: $\frac{n^2 + n - n^2}{\sqrt{n^2+n} + n} = \frac{n}{\sqrt{n^2+n} + n} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + 1/n} + 1} \to \frac12$.
notes: An $\infty - \infty$ form can still have a limit.
Forgets the factor 2 in the denominator.
facts: Rationalise an $\infty - \infty$ form with square roots.

en.q: A committee of 5 is to be chosen from 6 men and 4 women so that it includes at least 2 women. The number of ways is:
notes: Counts only the case of exactly 2 women.
Overcounts: ${}^4C_2 \times {}^8C_3$ counts some committees several times.
facts: 'At least' problems: add the separate cases, or subtract the unwanted cases from the total.

en.q: For any three vectors $\vec a$, $\vec b$, $\vec c$, the scalar triple product $[\vec a + \vec b,\ \vec b + \vec c,\ \vec c + \vec a]$ equals:
en.explanation: $(\vec b + \vec c)\times(\vec c + \vec a) = \vec b\times\vec c + \vec b\times\vec a + \vec c\times\vec a$ (since $\vec c\times\vec c = \vec 0$). Dotting with $\vec a$ leaves only $\vec a\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c) = [\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$; dotting with $\vec b$ leaves only $\vec b\cdot(\vec c\times\vec a) = [\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$; every other term has a repeated vector and is 0. Total: $2[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$.
notes: Keeps the term from $\vec a$ only and misses $\vec b\cdot(\vec c\times\vec a)$.
That is the value of $[\vec a - \vec b,\ \vec b - \vec c,\ \vec c - \vec a]$, whose three vectors add up to $\vec 0$.
Assumes each of the three sums contributes one $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$; only two terms survive.
facts: $[\vec a + \vec b,\ \vec b + \vec c,\ \vec c + \vec a] = 2[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$, while $[\vec a - \vec b,\ \vec b - \vec c,\ \vec c - \vec a] = 0$.

en.q: The time of flight of a projectile thrown with velocity $u$ at an angle $\alpha$ to the horizontal (on a horizontal plane) is:
en.explanation: Vertically, $y = (u\sin\alpha)t - \frac12gt^2 = 0$ gives $t = \frac{2u\sin\alpha}{g}$, twice the time to the greatest height.
notes: This is the time to reach the greatest height.
facts: $T = \frac{2u\sin\alpha}{g}$, $H = \frac{u^2\sin^2\alpha}{2g}$, $R = \frac{u^2\sin2\alpha}{g}$.

en.q: The general solution of $\frac{dy}{dx} + y = e^{-x}$ is:
en.explanation: Linear with $P = 1$: IF $= e^{\int1\,dx} = e^x$. Then $\frac{d}{dx}(ye^x) = e^x\cdot e^{-x} = 1$, so $ye^x = x + C$.
notes: Wrong integrating factor: it is $e^{\int 1\,dx} = e^x$.
facts: $y' + Py = Q$: IF $= e^{\int P\,dx}$, and $y\cdot\text{IF} = \int Q\cdot\text{IF}\,dx + C$.

src.label: Expected TGT 3 · Q36 · asked in UP TGT 2013

en.q: Out of three athletic teams in a school, 21 players are in the cricket team, 26 players are in the hockey team and 29 players are in the football team. Out of them, 14 can play hockey and cricket, 15 can play hockey and football, 12 can play football and cricket, and 8 can play all the three games. How many players are there in all in the three teams?
notes: Adds the three teams without removing the overlaps.
This is the sum of the three pairwise overlaps.
facts: $n(A\cup B\cup C) = \sum n(A) - \sum n(A\cap B) + n(A\cap B\cap C)$.

en.q: If $x = a\cos^3t$ and $y = a\sin^3t$, then $\frac{dy}{dx}$ equals:
en.explanation: $\frac{dx}{dt} = -3a\cos^2t\sin t$, $\frac{dy}{dt} = 3a\sin^2t\cos t$. $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{3a\sin^2t\cos t}{-3a\cos^2t\sin t} = -\tan t$.
notes: Misses the minus sign from $\frac{d}{dt}\cos t$.
facts: Parametric form: $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}$.

en.q: If $P(A) = 0.3$, $P(B) = 0.4$, $P(C) = 0.5$, $P(A \cap B) = 0.1$, $P(B \cap C) = 0.2$, $P(C \cap A) = 0.15$ and $P(A \cap B \cap C) = 0.05$, the probability that at least one of $A$, $B$, $C$ occurs is:
en.explanation: Addition theorem for three events: $P(A \cup B \cup C) = \Sigma P(A) - \Sigma P(A \cap B) + P(A \cap B \cap C) = 1.2 - 0.45 + 0.05 = 0.8$.
notes: Forgets to add back $P(A \cap B \cap C)$: $1.2 - 0.45$.
This is the probability that none occurs, $1 - 0.8$.
Subtracts $P(A \cap B \cap C)$ instead of adding it.
path: 16.1 Basic probability and the addition theorem
facts: $P(A \cup B \cup C) = \Sigma P(A) - \Sigma P(A \cap B) + P(A \cap B \cap C)$.

en.q: If $2^x = 3^y = 6^z$, where $x, y, z \ne 0$, then $z$ equals:
en.explanation: Let $2^x = 3^y = 6^z = k$ ($k \ne 1$ as the exponents are non-zero). Then $2 = k^{1/x}$, $3 = k^{1/y}$, $6 = k^{1/z}$. Since $6 = 2 \times 3$, $k^{1/z} = k^{1/x + 1/y}$, so $\frac1z = \frac1x + \frac1y = \frac{x + y}{xy}$ and $z = \frac{xy}{x + y}$.
notes: This is $\frac1z$; the reciprocal was not taken.
Adds the exponents, as if $6^{x+y}$ were $2^x \cdot 3^y$.
facts: If $a^x = b^y = (ab)^z$ (exponents non-zero), then $\frac1z = \frac1x + \frac1y$.

en.q: A non-empty finite subset $H$ of a group $G$ is a subgroup of $G$ if and only if:
en.explanation: If $H$ is finite and closed, each $a \in H$ has finite order $m$, so $a^m = e \in H$ and $a^{-1} = a^{m-1} \in H$. Thus closure alone makes a finite non-empty $H$ a subgroup; conversely every subgroup is closed.
notes: Inverses alone do not give closure.
Correct: for a finite subset, closure is enough.
Commutativity is not required for a subgroup.
Not enough: e.g. $\{e, a\}$ with $a^2 \ne e$.
facts: Finite $H \ne \varnothing$: subgroup $\iff$ closed. General $H$: subgroup $\iff ab^{-1} \in H$.

en.q: In a triangle $ABC$, if $a\cos^2\frac{C}{2} + c\cos^2\frac{A}{2} = \frac{3b}{2}$, then the sides $a, b, c$ are in:
en.explanation: $\cos^2\frac C2 = \frac{1+\cos C}{2}$, so the left side is $\frac{a + c + (a\cos C + c\cos A)}{2} = \frac{a + c + b}{2}$ by the projection formula $b = a\cos C + c\cos A$. Then $a + b + c = 3b$, i.e. $a + c = 2b$: the sides are in A.P.
facts: Projection formula: $b = a\cos C + c\cos A$.

en.q: If ${}^nP_r = {}^nP_{r+1}$ and ${}^nC_r = {}^nC_{r-1}$, then $(n, r)$ are:
en.explanation: ${}^nP_r = {}^nP_{r+1} \Rightarrow \frac{n!}{(n-r)!} = \frac{n!}{(n-r-1)!} \Rightarrow (n-r)! = (n-r-1)! \Rightarrow n - r = 1$. ${}^nC_r = {}^nC_{r-1} \Rightarrow r + (r-1) = n \Rightarrow n = 2r - 1$. Solving: $r = 2$, $n = 3$.

en.q: Let $y = |x| + |x - 2|$. Then the value of $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at $x = 2$ is:
en.explanation: For $0 < x < 2$: $y = x + (2 - x) = 2$, slope 0. For $x > 2$: $y = 2x - 2$, slope 2. The left derivative 0 differs from the right derivative 2, so $\frac{dy}{dx}$ does not exist at $x = 2$.
notes: This is only the left-hand derivative.
This is only the right-hand derivative.
Correct: left and right derivatives differ.
facts: $|x - a|$ has a corner at $x = a$: not differentiable there.

en.q: The equation of the bisectors of the angles between the lines $ax^2 + 2hxy + by^2 = 0$ is:
en.explanation: Let the lines make angles $\theta_1, \theta_2$ with the $x$-axis; their slopes satisfy $m_1 + m_2 = -\frac{2h}{b}$, $m_1m_2 = \frac ab$, so $\tan(\theta_1 + \theta_2) = \frac{m_1 + m_2}{1 - m_1m_2} = \frac{2h}{a - b}$. A bisector makes angle $\phi = \frac{\theta_1 + \theta_2}{2}$ (or $\phi + 90^\circ$), and for a point $(x, y)$ on it $\tan2\phi = \frac{2xy}{x^2 - y^2}$. Equating: $\frac{2xy}{x^2 - y^2} = \frac{2h}{a - b}$, i.e. $\frac{x^2 - y^2}{a - b} = \frac{xy}{h}$.
notes: Uses $a + b$ (the term in the angle formula).
facts: Bisectors of $ax^2 + 2hxy + by^2 = 0$: $\frac{x^2 - y^2}{a-b} = \frac{xy}{h}$.

en.q: If $\alpha, \beta$ are the roots of the equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$, then the equation whose roots are $\frac{1}{\alpha+\beta}$ and $\frac1\alpha + \frac1\beta$ is:
en.explanation: $\alpha + \beta = -\frac ba$, $\alpha\beta = \frac ca$. New roots: $\frac{1}{\alpha+\beta} = -\frac ab$ and $\frac1\alpha + \frac1\beta = \frac{\alpha+\beta}{\alpha\beta} = -\frac bc$. Sum $= -\frac{ac + b^2}{bc}$, product $= \frac ac$. Equation: $x^2 + \frac{b^2+ac}{bc}x + \frac ac = 0$, i.e. $bcx^2 + (b^2+ac)x + ab = 0$.
notes: Test $x^2 - 3x + 2 = 0$ (roots 1, 2; new roots $\frac13$, $\frac32$): this gives $-3x^2 + x + 2 = 0$, with roots 1 and $-\frac23$.
Same test: $2x^2 + 10x - 6 = 0$, whose roots are not $\frac13$ and $\frac32$.
Sign slip: the sum of the new roots is negative.
path: 1.8 Quadratic equations and theory of equations
facts: An equation with roots $p, q$: $x^2 - (p+q)x + pq = 0$.

en.q: The probability of Pragati solving a problem is $\frac13$ and that of Tripti is $\frac12$. If they try independently, what will be the probability of solving that problem?
en.explanation: $P(\text{not solved}) = \left(1 - \frac13\right)\left(1 - \frac12\right) = \frac23 \times \frac12 = \frac13$. Hence $P(\text{solved}) = 1 - \frac13 = \frac23$.
notes: This is the probability that neither solves it.
This is the probability that both solve it.
path: 16.2 Conditional probability, multiplication theorem, independent events
facts: For independent events, $P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - P(\bar A)P(\bar B)$.

en.q: Two like parallel forces of 6 N and 4 N act at points A and B, where AB = 10 cm. Their resultant acts at a point C on AB such that AC equals:
en.explanation: The resultant, 10 N, divides AB internally in the inverse ratio of the forces: $6\cdot AC = 4\cdot CB$ with $AC + CB = 10$. So $AC = 4$ cm, $CB = 6$ cm.
notes: Uses the rule for unlike forces (external division).
The resultant is not at the mid-point of unequal forces.
Correct: C is nearer the larger force.
path: 15.3 Coplanar forces, moments and parallel forces
facts: Like parallel forces $P, Q$: resultant $P + Q$ at C with $P\cdot AC = Q\cdot CB$.

en.q: The sum of all the $n$th roots of unity ($n \ge 2$) is:
en.explanation: The $n$th roots are $1, \omega, \omega^2, \dots, \omega^{n-1}$ with $\omega = e^{2\pi i/n} \ne 1$. Their sum is $\frac{1 - \omega^n}{1 - \omega} = 0$ (also, the coefficient of $z^{n-1}$ in $z^n - 1$ is 0).
notes: Adds the roots as if each were 1.
The product, not the sum, is $\pm1$.
This is the sum of the non-real cube roots, $\omega + \omega^2$.
path: 10.4 Polar form, Euler's form and De Moivre's theorem
facts: Sum of the $n$th roots of unity is 0; their product is $(-1)^{n-1}$.

en.q: If $A$ is a square matrix of order 3 and $|A| = 4$, then $|2A|$ equals:
en.explanation: Multiplying an $n \times n$ matrix by $k$ multiplies every row by $k$, so $|kA| = k^n|A|$. Here $|2A| = 2^3 \times 4 = 32$.
notes: Takes $|2A| = 2|A|$; each of the 3 rows gets the factor 2.
facts: $|kA| = k^n|A|$ for an $n \times n$ matrix.

en.q: If $\theta$ is the acute angle between two lines with slopes $m_1$ and $m_2$ ($m_1m_2 \ne -1$), then $\tan\theta$ equals:
en.explanation: If the lines make angles $\alpha, \beta$ with the $x$-axis ($m_1 = \tan\alpha$, $m_2 = \tan\beta$), the angle between them is $\alpha - \beta$ and $\tan(\alpha - \beta) = \frac{m_1 - m_2}{1 + m_1m_2}$. Taking the modulus gives the acute angle.
facts: Lines are parallel if $m_1 = m_2$ and perpendicular if $m_1m_2 = -1$.

en.q: The area of the region bounded by the curve $y = \tan x$, the tangent to it at $x = \frac{\pi}{4}$ and the $x$-axis is:
en.explanation: At $x = \frac{\pi}{4}$: $y = 1$ and $\frac{dy}{dx} = \sec^2\frac{\pi}{4} = 2$, so the tangent is $y - 1 = 2\left(x - \frac{\pi}{4}\right)$, meeting the $x$-axis at $x = \frac{\pi}{4} - \frac12$. The curve is convex on $\left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$, so the tangent lies below it. Area $= \int_0^{\pi/4}\tan x\,dx - \frac12 \cdot \frac12 \cdot 1 = \log_e\sec\frac{\pi}{4} - \frac14 = \frac12\log_e 2 - \frac14$ sq. units.
notes: Correct: area under the curve from $0$ to $\frac{\pi}{4}$ minus the triangle under the tangent.
Area under the curve only: the triangle under the tangent is not taken away.
Adds the triangle (base $\frac12$, height 1) instead of taking it away.
facts: $\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan x\,dx = \log_e\sqrt2 = \frac12\log_e 2$; a tangent to a convex curve lies below it, so the region between curve, tangent and axis is (area under the curve) − (triangle under the tangent).
